text: Preface The Commentary on the Constitution on the Church here offered to the public is an attempt to provide within the limits of a single moderately-sized and moderately-priced volume a fairly compre- hensive introduction to the document which marks the main achievement of the Second Vatican Council.
text_raw:
Preface 
The Commentary on the Constitution on the Church here offered 
to the public is an attempt to provide within the limits of a single 
moderately-sized and moderately-priced volume a fairly compre- 
hensive introduction to the document which marks the main 
achievement of the Second Vatican Council.

chapter_title: Part II Commentary on Lumen Gentium
text: Two objectives in particular have determined the planning and composition of the work: to present, at least in outline, a survey of the history of ecclesiology in the modern period, some insight into which is indispensable for an intelligent approach to the Constitu- tion; and, secondly, to provide an accurate and objective exposition of the conciliar text in the light of its genesis and in the context of contemporary theological discussion.

text: The importance accorded the episcopal office by Vatican II is not meant to result in making the bishop a kind of little pope in his own diocese, but rather is to be understood as reflecting the importance of the Church of God entrusted to his care: ‘Each individual bishop represents his own Church, but all of them together in union with the pope represent the entire Church joined in the bond of peace, love and unity.’ The local bishop, however, can faithfully represent his Church within the college of bishops only if he knows it, only if he guides and directs it in close union with his priests and faithful.

text: Anyone who is inclined to think that the senate of priests and the pastoral council of the laity are simply features of a novel contemporary drive to make the Church more democratic in her institutions has a good deal to learn from St Cyprian: ‘I have made it a rule ever since the beginning of my episcopate’, he says, ‘to make no decision merely on the strength of my own personal opinion without consulting you [i.e. the presbyters and deacons], without the approbation of the people.’ St Cyprian was well aware of something which the Church of our own time is discovering afresh: that leaders of the Church have no monopoly of the charisms and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

INTRODUCTION 
THE origin of chapter five of the Constitution is to be found in 
the fifth chapter of the original draft entitled ‘On the states for

text: Between the first and second sessions this chapter underwent fairly radical revision in the light of the criticisms which had been levelled against it.

text: The main purpose of the new draft, drawn up by a special group of bishops and theologians in May 1963 and submitted for debate by the Council the following October, was to set the re- ligious life, with which the chapter in its first form had been ex- clusively concerned, in its proper context in the mystery of the Church as a whole.

The main purpose of the new draft, drawn up by a special 
group of bishops and theologians in May 1963 and submitted for 
debate by the Council the following October, was to set the re- 
ligious life, with which the chapter in its first form had been ex- 
clusively concerned, in its proper context in the mystery of the 
Church as a whole.

text: It sought to remove the impression, all too easily derived from the original draft, that religious were a privileged élite called to a higher holiness than the general run of Christians and having access to more intimate union with Christ.} In order to make clear that there is but one holiness in the Church to which all Christians are called, no matter what their condition in life, the chapter was given a new title, ‘On the call to holiness in the Church’, and the treatment of religious was prefaced by an exposition of the universal vocation to holiness deriving from the Christian’s incorporation into Christ at baptism.

text: THE MEANING OF ESCHATOLOGY 301 Where Catholic theology put the emphasis on our union with God through the work of the incarnation in the past applied to us in space and time by the ministry of the institutional Church, and (as, for example, in a rather defective concept of the Church as the ‘continuation of the incarnation’) often tended to see this union in static terms, Protestant theology stated that we are united to God rather in ‘the act of the celestial Christ, spiritual and in- visible’.?

THE MEANING OF ESCHATOLOGY 301 
Where Catholic theology put the emphasis on our union with

text: It is based on union with Christ and possession of his Spirit, it means loving God and one’s neighbour and is expressed ‘in life within the Church, regular participation in the liturgy, etc. The chapter-ending points to the passing character of the world (and of the sacraments also), leading on to religious life as a sign of the ‘resurrected state and the glory of the heavenly kingdom.’ It signals the passing character of the ‘city’ here below, as well as ‘the surpassing greatness of the force of Christ the king and the boundless power of the Holy Spirit’.4 Thus all through the Constitution we find this reference of the present to the future, of the earthly to the heavenly, of the Church on earth to the final kingdom, yet a careful insistence on the importance of earthly life in Christ, not so much to gain entrance into heaven, as to give glory to God and to spread his kingdom among men.

for the Church as a whole.

text: Strictly collegiate acts will always be the exception, and their value and efficacy will depend very much on the vitality of what may be called the ordinary exercise of collegiality among the dioceses of the world, and in particular between the bishops throughout the world and the Roman pontiff.

Strictly collegiate acts will always be 
the exception, and their value and efficacy will depend very much 
on the vitality of what may be called the ordinary exercise of 
collegiality among the dioceses of the world, and in particular 
between the bishops throughout the world and the Roman pontiff.

text: Hoc vero religiosum voluntatis et intellectus obsequium singu- lari ratione praestandum est Romani Pontificis authentico magisterio etiam cum non ex cathedra loquitur; ita nempe ut magisterium eius supremum reverenter agnoscatur, et sententiis ab eo prolatis sincere adhaereatur, iuxta mentem et voluntatem manifestatam ipsius, quae se prodit praecipue sive indole documentorum, sive ex frequenti propo- sitione etusdem doctrinae, sive ex dicendi ratione.

text: Virgo in Ecclesia, titulis Advocatae, Auxiliatricis, Adiutricis, Mediatricis in- vocatur.* Quod tamen ita intelligitur, ut dignitati et efficacitati Christi unius Mediatoris nihil deroget, nihil superaddat.3 Nulla enim creatura cum Verbo incarnato ac Redemptore connume- rari umquam potest; sed sicut sacerdotium Christi variis modis tum a ministris tum a fideli populo participatur, et sicut una bonitas Dei in creaturis modis diversis realiter diffunditur, ita etiam unica mediatio Redemptoris non excludit, sed suscitat variam apud creaturas partici- patam ex unico fonte cooperationem.
